name: France

facts.religion: Catholic about 45%, Muslim about 8%, no religion about 35%

snapshot: Weeks of student-led protests over schools and living costs turned to riots in October, and the National Assembly unanimously rejected Sébastien Lecornu's 2027 budget.
culture: France has long been a global reference for food, wine, fashion, philosophy and cinema, and it is the world's most visited country. Laïcité, a strict separation of religion and state, shapes debates over headscarves in schools. The Tour de France, Cannes and the restored Notre-Dame, reopened in 2024, are national rituals.
society: France has a large welfare state funded by Europe's highest tax burden, and a deficit and debt that markets watch nervously. Pension reform triggered huge protests in 2023. Tensions over immigration, Islam and the banlieues fuel support for the National Rally. It is the EU's only nuclear-armed state and gets most of its power from nuclear reactors.
situation: France's Fifth Republic was designed in 1958 by Charles de Gaulle to end the chaos of the Fourth, which went through more than 20 governments in 12 years. For six decades it worked. Then in 2024 Emmanuel Macron called a snap election that left parliament split into three hostile blocs, and the old instability returned: prime ministers fell one after another, including Sébastien Lecornu's first government in October 2025, which lasted 14 hours before Macron reappointed him four days later (AFP via eNCA).

In 2026 Lecornu, 39, did what his predecessors could not: he survived. He got a 2026 budget passed in February after beating off a string of no-confidence motions, though at the price of giving up any serious attempt to cut France's deficit (The Local). In the March municipal elections the National Rally failed to take any major city. Now the country's attention has moved to the presidential election in spring 2027, when Macron must leave after two terms and the far right sees its best ever chance. Marine Le Pen, convicted of embezzling EU funds in 2025, was expected to be barred, with her 30-year-old protégé Jordan Bardella running instead; by August, Euronews reported Bardella had stepped back behind Le Pen (Euronews). The centre is crowded with would-be successors: Gabriel Attal, endorsed by Macron's party in May, Édouard Philippe, Bruno Retailleau and even former president François Hollande. Lecornu insists he is not running: "I don't know what language I need to say it in!"
power: A semi-presidential republic. The directly elected president, limited to two five-year terms, controls foreign and defence policy and appoints the prime minister, who needs the tolerance of the 577-seat National Assembly. With no majority in the Assembly, every government can fall to a censure vote.
holders: President Emmanuel Macron, until May 2027; Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu.

update.html: Protests that began in September over under-resourced high schools grew into a national movement over wages and living costs. On 17 October more than half a million people marched, and riots in Paris, Marseille, Lille and Limoges led to about 1,800 arrests and left more than 500 police, gendarmes and firefighters injured. On 4 November the National Assembly rejected the revenue part of the 2027 budget, which seeks 43 billion euros in savings, by 458 votes to none, sending it to the Senate and making it likely that Prime Minister Lecornu will force it through under Article 49.3 and face no-confidence votes. On 5 November between 575,000 people (government count) and 1.6 million (union count) joined a strike.
